implementation_notes: The one-line method is written as an expression body - public CancelResult Cancel(OrderId id) => _repo.Cancel(id); - and the read-only attribute form as an auto-property expression, public int Count => _repo.Count; The compiler emits the same accessor a block body would, so nothing is generated for you and no member is implied: what the language supplies is the one-expression member syntax, not a delegating-member mechanism, and the JIT (plus MethodImplOptions.AggressiveInlining) handles the cost. Keep expression bodies for members that really are one delegation; a body that grows a second statement should become a block, because the arrow hides the growth from reviewers.
pitfalls: An expression-bodied member is not a lambda: it compiles to an ordinary method, so adding async to a one-line forwarder that returns a Task allocates a state machine and changes where exceptions are observed.
A forwarding property is evaluated on every access; if the delegate's value is expensive or lazily built, the one-liner moved that cost into every caller.
MethodImplOptions.AggressiveInlining on an interface implementation or virtual member cannot help - the runtime decides - so do not treat the attribute as a guarantee.
